analysis.one_liner: Requires every new gun sold in the US to etch its identity onto fired cartridge casings, to help solve shootings.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in April 2006 and died there when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007, with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required that every firearm manufactured in or imported into the United States carry a 'microstamp' — an etched code of its make, model, and serial number on internal parts, so that every cartridge casing fired from the gun carries that identity. Gunmakers or importers who shipped non-microstamped guns would have their federal licenses revoked. It also directed the Justice Department to ballistics-test every gun in federal custody suspected of being used in a crime, build an electronic database of the results that state and local police could search, and report each year on how well the records helped investigations, with $20 million a year authorized for fiscal 2006 through 2009.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people affected by gun crime. When a cartridge casing is recovered at a shooting scene, a microstamp would link it directly to the registered buyer of the gun without needing the gun itself, and the ballistics database would let local police trace crime guns faster. The aim is quicker arrests and prosecutions in shootings.

how_it_helps.text: Every gun would have to imprint its make, model, and serial number onto cartridge casings fired from it, so casings recovered at crime scenes could point investigators to the gun's purchaser without recovering the weapon.

The Attorney General would have to ballistics-test any federally held firearm suspected of use in a crime and put the results in an electronic database that state and local law enforcement could promptly access, replacing slower manual tracing across jurisdictions.
The bill authorized $20,000,000 per fiscal year for 2006 through 2009 to build and operate the ballistics-testing system.
An importer or manufacturer that shipped a non-microstamped gun would lose its federal firearms license, giving the mandate real teeth.

analysis.who_pays: Firearms manufacturers and importers, who would have to redesign guns to embed microstamping technology, and by extension gun buyers through prices. Taxpayers would fund the $20 million-a-year ballistics database.

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers would bear the cost of retooling firearms to include microstamping elements, a cost that would likely be passed to buyers through higher gun prices.
The mandate targets lawful production, not the existing stock of millions of guns already in circulation, so it would have little effect on crime guns for years after enactment.

Ballistics identification is imperfect: markings on casings can change as a firing mechanism wears, and the bill's own reporting requirement appears to anticipate the need to measure how valuable the records actually are in real prosecutions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a modest, technology-based way to solve gun crimes faster, with the compliance burden falling on an industry rather than on taxpayers in the main. Its limits are real: it could not touch the millions of unmarked guns already owned, and microstamping's usefulness depends on the technology staying intact and reliable. It was a narrow tool, not a broad crime or gun policy.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee in April 2006, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when that Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Andrews introduced the TRACE Act on April 3, 2006.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary, which was the only committee referral it received.
No further action was ever taken: the bill had no cosponsors and the full action history ends with the committee referral, so it died in committee when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms manufacturers and importers are better off, because they never faced the microstamping mandate or license-revocation risk. Agencies investigating gun crimes gained nothing, since the ballistics database was never built under this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun manufacturers, who faced no mandate

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Andrews
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; it attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no markup, no vote, no report.

against.name: Rep. F. James Sensenbrenner
against.what_they_did: As committee chair during the 109th Congress, never scheduled the bill for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a single Democrat, drew zero cosponsors from either party, and died in committee under Republican control of the House in the 109th Congress.

industries.note: The bill would have required every gun they made or imported to carry a microstamp, with license revocation as the penalty for noncompliance. Avoiding the mandate preserved their existing production methods and costs.
Compliance costs would likely raise prices, but dealers also benefit when crime guns are traced quickly rather than implicating their sales. The bill imposed no direct requirements on dealers.
